A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCAR study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V5 reports original stylometric analyses, ranker evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, and ablations on coding and open-domain tasks.

after.justification: V7 retains original experiments and adds filtered-response experiments, capability evaluations, and bias analyses.

M1.justification: The ranker architecture, quality-constrained ranking loss, triplet representation losses, and top-percentage selection procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 explicitly states that the new perplexity filtering is not applied to SCAR training.

E1.justification: V7 retains the coding and AlpacaEval coverage and adds ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, MMLU, and TruthfulQA evaluations (C.7). WinoBias- and BOLD-based evaluations additionally test toxicity and sentiment across demographic and occupational groups (E.1), substantially broadening task coverage.

E2.justification: V7 adds Longest, which selects responses by token length, to the coding and open-domain comparisons while retaining the six earlier baselines. Its participation is verified in Tables 8–10; on 50% synthetic open-domain data, it scores 6.29 versus SCAR(ID)'s 5.56.

E3.justification: Section 2 introduces surprisal-matching filters, reducing 10,000 StackExchange and 1,000 LIMA examples to 944 and 407, with unfiltered results retained in B.3. The main style analysis switches from semantic-token perplexity to full-response perplexity and adds layout frequency. New capability and bias evaluations introduce additional scoring protocols, although C.7 gives conflicting descriptions of TruthfulQA scoring.

E4.justification: V7 adds filtered-versus-unfiltered analysis (B.3), regression and variance analyses testing the relationship between linguistic form and surprisal (B.4), and fairness and instruction/response lexical-diversity analyses (E). Existing component ablations and representation-similarity analyses remain; removing synthetic panels from Figure 3 does not remove their tabulated results.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 adds regression-based feature-importance estimation and variance-contribution estimates beyond v5's descriptive statistics and CMI analysis. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the stylometric standard deviations describe variation across responses.

E6.justification: V5's unfiltered coding Avg. Pass@1 scores of 31.65 for human responses and 35.11 for GPT-3.5 direct responses survive in v7 Table 6. V7 Table 1 adds 26.56 and 31.00 under the filtered setting, so these are not same-setting performance declines. Longest, capability, bias, and lexical-diversity results substantially expand the evidence, while corresponding existing coding-selection and ablation scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The ranking, reward, triplet-loss, and CMI equations are mathematically unchanged. Appendix B.5 adds standard surprisal and probability-chain-rule background, without a substantive new derivation, proof, or formal guarantee.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that style consistency improves fine-tuning at comparable data quality and that SCAR can match or exceed full-dataset performance using as little as 0.7% of the data. Renaming semantic surprisal to instructional surprisal and consolidating three contribution bullets into two preserve these core claims.

C2.justification: V7 adds interpretations of feature independence and explanations for distributed, nonlinear surprisal representations (B.4–B.5), plus substantive fairness and lexical-diversity limitations. Section 4.1 replaces v5's broad reduced-diversity argument with a scenario-dependent balance and interprets Longest's competitiveness through response style. The new fairness discussion is optimistic despite mixed outcomes in Table 19.

D1.justification: V7 newly specifies a 2048-token input limit, a SentenceBERT checkpoint, and evaluation-tool details. It omits v5's explicit 8:1:1 ranker split, zero generation temperature, and guesslang preprocessing disclosure. Core training hyperparameters, generation prompts, and the code/data access link remain.

R1.justification: V7 adds length-based selection, embedding, capability-benchmark, and bias-related references, and expands its comparison with prior surprisal modeling in B.5. It removes Section 2's explicit discussion contrasting semantic and non-semantic definitions of style. The central positioning relative to LIMA and existing data-selection approaches remains.

P1.justification: V7 extensively reorganizes the flat appendix into thematic sections A–F with a contents page, moves examples and ranker analysis out of the main text, and replaces standalone reproducibility/ethics statements with a limitations section. Terminology and substantial explanatory passages are also revised.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with widespread figure and table relocation. Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 2 gains Longest, and Figure 3 contracts from four panels to two. New capability and bias tables and revised stylometric columns substantially change the presentation.

improvement.justification: V7 better tests the central style hypothesis through surprisal-matched controls and strengthens comparison through Longest and broader evaluations. These benefits are tempered by conflicting TruthfulQA scoring descriptions, overstrong independence interpretations, and lost reproducibility details. Tables 14 and 19 also reveal MMLU declines and toxicity increases that receive insufficient discussion, limiting the net quality gain.
